passage: Fifteen minutes before opening, Simran had to show Manjula, the new hire, how to record a returned item in the stock sheet. "What do you do when a customer buys something?" Simran asked. "I subtract one from the sheet," Manjula said. "Good. A return is the opposite." Simran did one example: a red kettle back, plus one. "Now explain it back to me, as if I'm the customer." Manjula frowned, explained, and got the sign wrong. Simran did not sigh. "Try the next return." A blue mug: Manjula added one and typed it correctly. The shutter went up on time, and the first return of the day was Manjula's, done alone.

qa.q: What was the item in Simran's example return?
qa.a: It was a red kettle.

qa.q: What might Simran have wanted when asking Manjula to explain it back?
qa.a: Simran wanted to check that Manjula really understood, not just nodded, and stayed patient despite the ticking clock.

qa.q: What made the explain-back step useful?
qa.a: It showed the sign error early, before a real customer, and gave Manjula a chance to fix it with the next return.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt on getting the sign wrong and not being sighed at?
qa.a: Probably nervous but reassured, able to try again because Simran stayed patient. 🙂

grounding: Shows an explainer starting from what the learner knows, giving one example and asking for it back in the learner's words.

passage: In the office store room, Anand slid a blank delivery form towards Lokesh, the new intern. "Have you ever written a receipt at your uncle's shop?" "Yes, every Sunday." "This is the same, plus one line for who signs." Anand filled one in for a box of files and read it aloud. Lokesh nodded quickly. "Great. Now tell me in your own words what goes where." Lokesh explained it, put the signature line under the date, and stopped. "Try the next one alone," Anand said, handing over two boxes. Lokesh's first form had the address in the wrong box. They fixed it together. By the fourth form Lokesh needed no help.

qa.q: Where had Lokesh written receipts before?
qa.a: Lokesh had written receipts at an uncle's shop every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Anand hope to find out by asking Lokesh to explain in Lokesh's own words?
qa.a: Whether Lokesh had really understood, since a nod alone does not show it.

qa.q: Why was giving a small task better than accepting a quick nod?
qa.a: The wrong box showed up on the first form while Anand was there to fix it, so the mistake was caught in practice and not later.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt about the address in the wrong box?
qa.a: Slightly embarrassed but relieved it was caught during practice with Anand there to help.

grounding: Shows an explainer starting from familiar experience, giving one example, asking for it back and setting a small task to test understanding.

passage:
"Arohi, you've used a grocery list, right?" Naveen pulled a chair next to hers.
"Obviously."
"Then you already know how the stock sheet works. Each row is an item. This column is what we have. This one is the minimum. If 'have' drops below 'minimum,' it turns red and we reorder."
"Okay."
"One example. Printer paper: we have four, the minimum is ten. Red. So?"
"We order."
"How many?"
Arohi paused. "Up to… the maximum column?"
"Yes. Now explain the whole thing back to me, in your words, like I'm new."
She laughed. "Rows are things. If the number's below the minimum, it goes red, and we order back up to the maximum."
"Perfect. Now, small task. The sheet has three reds today. Tell me what to order."
Arohi scrolled. "Toner, two… paper, six… wait, why is the tea red?"
"Because it's always red," Naveen said. "Good. You've got it."

qa.q: How many printer paper packs does the example say they have?
qa.a: We have four, the minimum is ten.

qa.q: How did Arohi seem to feel when asked to explain it back?
qa.a: Arohi felt amused and a little shy, laughing, then confident as she explained it in her own words.

qa.q: Which steps did Naveen use to check that Arohi understood?
qa.a: Naveen started from a grocery list, gave one example, asked Arohi to explain it back and then gave a small real task.

qa.q: How does Naveen feel when Arohi spots the red tea?
qa.a: Naveen is pleased and amused, since noticing the tea shows Arohi is really reading the sheet.

grounding: Illustrates an explainer who starts from what the learner knows, gives one example, asks for it back in her words and sets a small task.

passage:
For my first year as a café manager, I trained people by asking, "Got it?" They always said yes. Then they closed the till wrong.
Last month, Anjali joined. Before I showed her anything, I asked what she already knew. She had worked in her uncle's shop, counting cash at night. So I said, "Closing the till is your uncle's shop, plus one screen."
I showed her one full close, slowly. Then, instead of "Got it?", I said, "Tell me the steps back, your way." She got four out of five. She'd missed printing the summary. We fixed that.
Then I gave her a small task: close the morning till while I watched and didn't speak. She did it with only one pause.
I'm Jeevan, and I used to think nodding meant understanding. It mostly means someone is being polite. Now I only trust what I've seen someone do.

qa.q: Where had Anjali worked before?
qa.a: She had worked in her uncle's shop, counting cash at night.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel now about the old "Got it?" habit?
qa.a: Jeevan feels a little rueful and embarrassed about it, seeing that nods were only politeness and led to wrong till closes.

qa.q: Which part of Jeevan's method showed whether the training worked?
qa.a: The small task, closing the morning till while Jeevan watched silently, because it showed what Anjali could actually do.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when her uncle's shop was used as the starting point?
qa.a: Anjali probably felt reassured and capable, since the new job was linked to something she already knew.

grounding: Shows an explainer who starts from what the learner knows, gives one example, asks for it back and sets a small task to check.

passage:
Team lead's note, customer support floor, Thursday.
I watched Uma train our new hire, Parul, on the refund process today, and I want to record it.
Uma began by asking Parul what she already knew. Parul had returned things online herself, so Uma said, "Good, you've been the customer. Now you're the other side."
Uma walked through one real refund slowly. She didn't show five. Then she asked, "Explain it to me as if I'm the next new person." Parul explained well but missed the step of checking the order date. Uma didn't correct her immediately; she asked, "What if the order is three months old?" Parul thought and found the gap herself.
Then Uma gave her one live ticket and sat back with her hands in her lap. Parul finished it in six minutes, correctly.
Most trainers ask, "Any doubts?" and accept silence. I will ask Uma to show the others this method next week.
— Team lead, Support

qa.q: How long did Parul take to finish the live ticket?
qa.a: Parul finished it in six minutes, correctly.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt when she found the gap herself?
qa.a: Parul probably felt proud and more confident, since she worked out the missing step instead of being told.

qa.q: Why did Uma ask a question instead of correcting Parul straight away?
qa.a: Asking about an old order let Parul spot the missing step herself, which checks and deepens understanding.

qa.q: How does the team lead see Uma's way of training?
qa.a: The team lead admires it, contrasting it with trainers who accept silence, and plans to have Uma show the others.

grounding: Illustrates an explainer who starts from the learner's experience, gives one example, asks for it back and sets a small task.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Rehana's third day at the bakery. Yesterday I explained proofing for ten minutes and she nodded through all of it, then left the trays too close to the oven and the dough went slack. My fault as much as hers.
Today I tried it differently. First I asked what she already knew. "I make rotis at home. I let the atta rest." Perfect, so I began there: resting roti dough and proofing bread are cousins, both need time, only here it's more warmth and more time.
One example only. I pressed a finger into a risen bun and showed her how the dent springs back halfway, slowly.
Then I asked her to tell it back to me. She said, "It's ready when it pushes back a bit. Not fully, not never." Better than my version!
Then the real test: she checked the second tray alone. Called it right 🙂
Note to self: nodding means nothing. The tray tells the truth.
Jaya

qa.q: What did Rehana say she does at home?
qa.a: She makes rotis at home and lets the atta rest.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel about the first day's explanation?
qa.a: Jaya felt guilty and partly to blame, writing "My fault as much as hers" after ten minutes of nodding hid that Rehana had not understood.

qa.q: Which steps in Jaya's new approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Starting from Rehana's roti dough, giving one finger-press example, asking her to say it back, and letting her check a tray alone showed whether it had really landed.

qa.q: What might the second day have been like for Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt more confident, because the lesson began with something she knew and she got to prove it by judging the tray herself.

grounding: Shows an explainer starting from what the learner knows, using one example, and checking understanding with a small real task.
